mainEntity.name: What causes erectile dysfunction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common causes are reduced blood flow, nerve damage, hormonal problems, medicines, psychological factors and surgery in the pelvic area. Many men have more than one cause.

mainEntity.name: Can ED be a sign of another health problem?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. ED shares risk factors with heart disease and diabetes and can be an early warning sign, so a health review is sensible, particularly if ED is new or getting worse.

mainEntity.name: Do I need tests for ED?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. The doctor decides after your history and examination. Blood tests are common, and penile Doppler ultrasound is used in selected men to assess blood flow.

mainEntity.name: Is ED permanent?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the cause. Some causes can be treated or improved, while others need long-term management. A specialist assessment gives a more realistic picture for your case.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to know which treatment I want before contacting the clinic?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Send your case and the clinic can advise which options may be relevant to you.

mainEntity.name: Is the P-Shot proven to treat erectile dysfunction?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Some trials report improvement, while others found no difference from placebo. The 2026 European Association of Urology (EAU) guideline says intracavernosal PRP for erectile dysfunction should be used only in a clinical-trial setting.

mainEntity.name: Does the P-Shot hurt?

acceptedAnswer.text: Numbing is used before the injection. Many men describe mild discomfort, but experiences differ.

mainEntity.name: Is the P-Shot permanent?

acceptedAnswer.text: No permanent effect can be promised. If there is a benefit, how long it lasts is uncertain and varies between patients.

mainEntity.name: Is the P-Shot safe?

acceptedAnswer.text: Reported side effects have mostly been minor, but studies are small and long-term data are limited. The doctor explains the risks and who should not have it.

mainEntity.name: Does the P-Shot increase penis size?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. P-Shot is not a penile-enlargement treatment and the clinic does not claim it enlarges the penis.

mainEntity.name: Can I have P-Shot together with other treatments?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes the doctor may discuss combinations, but evidence is limited. Treatment is decided after assessment.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between P-Shot and PRP for ED?

acceptedAnswer.text: P-Shot is a brand-style name for penile PRP injection. The medical term is intracavernosal platelet-rich plasma injection.

schema.name: P-Shot (platelet-rich plasma injection)
schema.description: P-Shot is a penile PRP procedure in which platelet-rich plasma prepared from the patient's own blood is injected into penile tissue. It is used by some clinics as a regenerative approach for selected men with erectile dysfunction. It is considered experimental, and suitability and expected benefit vary between patients.

schema.name: How is PRP prepared and the P-Shot performed?

itemListElement.name: Assessment and consent
itemListElement.description: The urologist reviews your history and examines you, and explains the evidence, risks and alternatives. You sign written consent before treatment.

itemListElement.name: Blood sample
itemListElement.description: A small amount of blood is taken from your arm using a sterile technique.

itemListElement.name: PRP preparation
itemListElement.description: The blood is spun in a centrifuge. This separates the plasma and concentrates the platelets into platelet-rich plasma.

itemListElement.name: Numbing
itemListElement.description: Local anaesthetic or numbing cream is used so the injection is more comfortable.

itemListElement.name: Injection
itemListElement.description: The PRP is injected into penile tissue by the doctor. It is an outpatient procedure, so you go home the same day.

itemListElement.name: Aftercare
itemListElement.description: You receive written aftercare instructions, warning signs and a contact for questions.

mainEntity.name: Does low testosterone cause erectile dysfunction?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can contribute, but ED is not proof of deficiency. Diagnosis requires compatible symptoms and appropriately timed biochemical testing, usually confirmed on more than one occasion.

mainEntity.name: Will testosterone therapy cure my ED?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. It can improve sexual symptoms in men with confirmed hypogonadism but does not repair established vascular or nerve damage.

mainEntity.name: Is PRP combined with testosterone more effective?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no high-quality evidence establishing that combination as superior, so it should not be marketed as synergistic without a relevant, cited clinical trial.

mainEntity.name: Can finasteride cause erectile dysfunction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Finasteride is associated with sexual side effects including ED and reduced libido, and UK safety information warns that sexual dysfunction may persist after treatment is stopped.

mainEntity.name: Is post-finasteride syndrome an established diagnosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: The regulator warning is clear, but the mechanisms, prevalence and boundaries of the broader label remain uncertain because of study design limitations.

mainEntity.name: Does PRP treat persistent sexual symptoms after finasteride?

acceptedAnswer.text: No credible evidence establishes PRP for this purpose, and treatments marketed as tissue repair should not be presented as proven for this condition.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if I have symptoms after finasteride?

acceptedAnswer.text: Discuss symptoms and medication history with the prescriber or a clinician experienced in sexual medicine, and do not restart, stop or change prescribed treatment based on a website. Seek urgent help for suicidal thoughts or marked mental-health deterioration.

mainEntity.name: Is the P-Shot better than Viagra?

acceptedAnswer.text: No evidence shows that. Viagra (sildenafil) has established evidence and guideline support as first-line therapy for many men, while PRP is experimental with inconsistent evidence.

mainEntity.name: What if Viagra does not seem to work?

acceptedAnswer.text: A clinician should check the likely cause, dose, timing, sexual stimulation, meal effects, medication authenticity and contraindications, because apparent non-response can reflect incorrect use or an untreated contributor.

mainEntity.name: Can I take Viagra with nitrates?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Sildenafil must not be combined with nitrates or nitric-oxide donors because of dangerous blood-pressure effects.
